facts.text: The Wicker Man was first released as the lower half of a double bill.

russmeyer.signature: The cartoonish king of American sexploitation.
russmeyer.description: A former combat cameraman who shot, edited and distributed his own films.

facts.text: Roger Ebert wrote the script of Beyond the Valley of the Dolls.

ryancoogler.signature: Brings personal, political feeling to franchise filmmaking.
ryancoogler.description: From Oakland. The actor Michael B. Jordan appears in all his features.

facts.text: Black Panther was the first superhero film nominated for the Best Picture Oscar.

sammendes.signature: A stage director with a taste for immaculate images.
sammendes.description: He works with star cinematographers such as Conrad Hall and Roger Deakins.

facts.text: 1917 is staged to look like one continuous shot.

samraimi.signature: A hyperactive camera and slapstick gore.
samraimi.description: He began with home-made horror in Michigan and went on to superhero blockbusters.

facts.text: Mounted the camera on a plank carried at a run for the demon's point of view in The Evil Dead.

samwood.description: A studio director from the silent era onward.

facts.text: Directed A Night at the Opera and A Day at the Races for the Marx Brothers.
Made The Apple at 17 with the real family whose story it tells.

sergiocorbucci.signature: The bleakest and most violent of the spaghetti western directors.
sergiocorbucci.description: His westerns are muddy, snowy and politically bitter.

facts.text: Directed the original Django (1966).

shadiabdelsalam.signature: One hieratic masterpiece about Egypt's ancient inheritance.

facts.text: Roberto Rossellini helped get The Night of Counting the Years made.

shirleyclarke.signature: A dancer who became a leader of the New York independent movement.
shirleyclarke.description: She blurred staged and documentary film.

facts.text: Co-founded the Film-Makers' Cooperative with Jonas Mekas.

stevejames.description: He follows his subjects over years with Chicago's Kartemquin Films.

facts.text: The Academy changed its documentary voting rules after Hoop Dreams was not nominated.

stuartrosenberg.signature: A television veteran with one enduring anti-authority classic.
stuartrosenberg.description: He often worked with Paul Newman.

facts.text: Cool Hand Luke was photographed by Conrad Hall.
Smithereens was the first American independent film selected for competition at Cannes.

suzanpitt.description: A painter who animated cel by cel.

facts.text: Asparagus played for about two years with Eraserhead at midnight screenings.

tminhhatrinh.signature: A theorist-filmmaker who dismantled the ethnographic film.

facts.text: Her narration in Reassemblage says she intends not to speak about, only to speak nearby.

tedkotcheff.signature: A journeyman with one great film about Australia.
tedkotcheff.description: A Canadian who worked in Britain, Australia and Hollywood.

facts.text: Later directed First Blood, the first Rambo film.

terryjones.description: A medieval historian as well as a comedian.

facts.text: Co-directed Monty Python and the Holy Grail with Terry Gilliam.

tomtykwer.signature: Kinetic experiments with chance and time.

facts.text: Run Lola Run tells the same twenty minutes three times.

tomasalfredson.description: He came from Swedish television comedy.

facts.text: The swimming-pool scene in Let the Right One In plays out underwater in a single shot.

toshiomatsumoto.signature: A theorist and pioneer of Japanese experimental film.
toshiomatsumoto.description: He mixed documentary, fiction and avant-garde techniques.

facts.text: Funeral Parade of Roses is said to have influenced Kubrick's A Clockwork Orange.

ulrikeottinger.signature: Extravagant costume fantasies and long ethnographic journeys.

facts.text: Designs her films' costumes and operates the camera herself.

valieexport.signature: A feminist performance artist who extended her actions into film.

facts.text: In Tap and Touch Cinema she wore a box 'cinema' over her chest in the street.

walterruttmann.signature: A pioneer of abstract film and of the city symphony.
walterruttmann.description: A painter who moved from animated abstraction to rhythmic documentary.

facts.text: Later worked on Nazi propaganda films, including as an adviser on Olympia.

warrenbeatty.signature: A star who became a producer, writer and director.
warrenbeatty.description: He directed only a handful of films.

facts.text: Reds interrupts its story with interviews with real witnesses of the period.

williamdieterle.signature: A German émigré at home in biography and romantic fantasy.
williamdieterle.description: He acted for Murnau before emigrating to Hollywood.

facts.text: Was known for wearing white gloves on set.

yurinorstein.description: He animates layered paper cut-outs on panes of glass with his wife, the artist Francheska Yarbusova.

facts.text: Has been working on The Overcoat since 1981.

zeinabuirenedavis.signature: A later member of the L.A. Rebellion.
zeinabuirenedavis.description: Her work centres on Black women's history.

facts.text: Compensation uses silent-film intertitles to tell two deaf-hearing love stories.

zelimirzilnik.signature: The docu-fiction guerrilla of the Yugoslav Black Wave.
zelimirzilnik.description: He has made low-budget films with marginalised people for over fifty years.

facts.text: Early Works won the Golden Bear in 1969.

alexanderhammid.signature: A Czech avant-gardist who co-made the most influential American experimental film.
alexanderhammid.description: Born Alexandr Hackenschmied in Linz, he was a photographer and filmmaker of the Czech avant-garde before emigrating to the United States, where he worked on documentaries and with Maya Deren.

facts.text: Co-directed Meshes of the Afternoon with Maya Deren, then his wife.
Co-directed the Oscar-winning short To Be Alive! for the 1964 New York World's Fair.

basilwright.signature: The most lyrical film-maker of the British documentary movement.
basilwright.description: A member of John Grierson's group at the Empire Marketing Board and the GPO Film Unit, he made poetic documentaries that set images against music and words.

facts.text: Song of Ceylon uses passages from a 17th-century English account of the island on its soundtrack.
Co-directed Night Mail, with verse by W. H. Auden and music by Benjamin Britten.

harrywatt.description: A GPO Film Unit director who staged real people in scripted scenes, a method he carried into wartime propaganda and then into feature films for Ealing.

facts.text: Target for Tonight, played by real RAF crews, received an honorary Oscar.
Made The Overlanders in Australia for Ealing.

hovdemeyer.signature: The editors who shaped Grey Gardens into a portrait.
hovdemeyer.description: Ellen Hovde and Muffie Meyer edited and co-directed Grey Gardens with Albert and David Maysles, then made documentaries together for decades.

facts.text: Grey Gardens credits four directors: the two Maysles brothers, Hovde and Meyer.

charlottezwerin.signature: The editor-director behind direct cinema's most famous rock film.
charlottezwerin.description: She edited and co-directed films with the Maysles brothers, including Salesman and Gimme Shelter, and later made portraits of musicians and artists.

facts.text: Gimme Shelter shows the Rolling Stones watching footage of the killing at Altamont.
Directed Thelonious Monk: Straight, No Chaser.

clydebruckman.signature: Keaton's gag writer and co-director of The General.
clydebruckman.description: A former sports reporter who wrote gags for Buster Keaton, Harold Lloyd and Laurel and Hardy, and co-directed some of their best films.

facts.text: Directed W. C. Fields in The Fatal Glass of Beer.
Directed Harold Lloyd in Feet First.

edwardsedgwick.signature: The MGM director of Keaton's last great silent comedies.
edwardsedgwick.description: A studio director of comedies and westerns who directed Buster Keaton's first films at MGM.

facts.text: Directed The Cameraman and Spite Marriage with Keaton at MGM.

donaldcrisp.signature: A Griffith actor who co-directed The Navigator.
donaldcrisp.description: Better known as an actor, he directed silent features in the 1910s and 1920s, including The Navigator with Buster Keaton and Don Q, Son of Zorro with Douglas Fairbanks.

facts.text: Played Ulysses S. Grant in The Birth of a Nation.
Won the Oscar for Best Supporting Actor for How Green Was My Valley.

charlesreisner.signature: Directed the cyclone of Steamboat Bill, Jr.
charlesreisner.description: A former vaudeville performer who worked with Chaplin and directed comedies for Buster Keaton, Syd Chaplin and later MGM.

facts.text: Plays the bully in Chaplin's The Kid.

johngblystone.description: A Fox studio director of comedies and adventure films for two decades.

facts.text: Directed Laurel and Hardy's Block-Heads, his last film.

hamiltonluske.signature: One of the sequence directors behind Disney's classic features.
hamiltonluske.description: An animator who became a sequence and supervising director on Disney features from Pinocchio to One Hundred and One Dalmatians.

facts.text: Shared the Oscar for special visual effects for Mary Poppins.

jeromerobbins.signature: The Broadway choreographer who co-directed West Side Story.
jeromerobbins.description: A leading choreographer of ballet and Broadway, he staged the dances of West Side Story and co-directed the film until he was taken off it during shooting.

facts.text: Shared the Best Director Oscar for West Side Story with Robert Wise, the first time the award was shared.

ludwigberger.signature: A Weimar specialist in fairy tale and operetta.
ludwigberger.description: A theatre director who made romantic costume films and musicals in Berlin, then worked in Hollywood, the Netherlands and Britain after 1933.

facts.text: Was hired to direct The Thief of Bagdad and was gradually replaced by Michael Powell and Tim Whelan.

timwhelan.signature: An American comedy writer who directed in Britain.
timwhelan.description: He wrote gags for Harold Lloyd and directed comedies and thrillers in Britain in the 1930s before co-directing The Thief of Bagdad.

facts.text: Co-wrote Harold Lloyd's The Freshman.

persichettiramseyrothman.signature: Made a superhero film look like a comic book in motion.
persichettiramseyrothman.description: A storyboard artist, an animation director and a comedy writer who co-directed Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse, mixing frame rates, halftone dots and comic panels.

facts.text: Into the Spider-Verse won the Oscar for Best Animated Feature; Ramsey was the first Black filmmaker to win that award.

serifgoren.signature: The director who shot Yol while its author was in prison.
serifgoren.description: A long-time assistant and editor for Yılmaz Güney who became a director in his own right, filming rural and working-class Turkey.

facts.text: Completed Güney's film Endişe (Anxiety) after Güney was jailed in 1974.
Shot Yol on location following Güney's script and written instructions.

stewartmcallister.description: A film editor at the Crown Film Unit whose cutting shaped Jennings's wartime films.

facts.text: Is credited as co-director of Listen to Britain.

williamkeighley.signature: A Warner Bros. contract director of gangster films and swashbucklers.
williamkeighley.description: A former stage director who made fast, efficient films for Warner Bros. in the 1930s, several with James Cagney.

facts.text: Began The Adventures of Robin Hood and was replaced by Michael Curtiz.

joshbennysafdie.signature: Panic attacks in movie form: New York hustlers filmed in long-lens close-up.
joshbennysafdie.description: Brothers from New York who began with micro-budget films cast partly with people found on the street, then made frantic crime films scored by Oneohtrix Point Never.

facts.text: Heaven Knows What stars Arielle Holmes playing a version of herself, from her own memoir.
Since 2025 they have directed separately: Josh made Marty Supreme and Benny The Smashing Machine.

ariaster.signature: Family grief staged as ritual horror.
ariaster.description: His films begin as domestic or relationship dramas and turn into rites of cult horror, framed with cold symmetry and long, gliding shots.

facts.text: Hereditary was his first feature.
Midsommar takes place almost entirely in daylight.

roberteggers.signature: Folk horror researched down to the dialect and the candlelight.
roberteggers.description: A former production designer whose films recreate historical worlds with obsessive accuracy, using period language and natural or candle light.

facts.text: The Witch's dialogue draws on 17th-century diaries and court records.
The Lighthouse was shot in black and white in a nearly square frame.

noahbaumbach.signature: Talky, wincing comedies of family and divorce in New York.
noahbaumbach.description: His films study articulate, self-absorbed New Yorkers through quick, overlapping dialogue, often drawing on his own family life.

facts.text: The Squid and the Whale draws on his parents' divorce.
Co-wrote Barbie with Greta Gerwig.

spikejonze.signature: A skate-video and music-video maker who made melancholy fables.
spikejonze.description: He moved from skateboard films and music videos to features that treat loneliness with whimsy, from Charlie Kaufman's puzzles to a love story with an operating system.

facts.text: Won the original screenplay Oscar for Her.
Co-created Jackass.

toddsolondz.description: His comedies of New Jersey suburbia treat loneliness, abuse and humiliation with a flat, unblinking deadpan.

facts.text: Welcome to the Dollhouse won the Grand Jury Prize at Sundance.

halhartley.signature: Deadpan Long Island romances, spoken like epigrams.
halhartley.description: His films of the late 1980s and 1990s use flat, aphoristic dialogue, repeated lines and choreographed gestures, with a regular company of actors.

facts.text: Composes much of his own film music, under the name Ned Rifle.

whitstillman.signature: Comedies of manners about the urban haute bourgeoisie.
whitstillman.description: His films follow articulate, preppy young people talking through love, class and morality, with a dry, Austen-like wit.

facts.text: Metropolitan was nominated for the original screenplay Oscar.

greggaraki.signature: Candy-coloured apocalypses of queer teenage angst.
greggaraki.description: A key figure of the New Queer Cinema whose films mix shoegaze and goth music, saturated colour and nihilistic humour.

facts.text: Totally F***ed Up, The Doom Generation and Nowhere form his Teen Apocalypse trilogy.

larryclark.signature: A photographer's raw look at teenage lives.
larryclark.description: His photo books documented drug use among his friends in Tulsa; his films cast real skateboarders and teenagers to show sex and drugs without moralising.

facts.text: His first photo book, Tulsa, was published in 1971.

debragranik.signature: Quiet portraits of Americans living off the grid.
debragranik.description: She films rural and marginal communities with local non-professionals and an unhurried attention to work and survival.

facts.text: Winter's Bone gave Jennifer Lawrence her first Oscar nomination.

jeffnichols.signature: Southern dramas where family love meets dread.
jeffnichols.description: From Arkansas, he makes restrained genre films about fathers and families in the American South.

facts.text: Michael Shannon appears in all his features.

treyedwardshults.signature: Family trauma filmed with a swirling, music-driven camera.
treyedwardshults.description: His films treat family conflict as an emergency, with long tracking shots, shifting aspect ratios and loud soundtracks.

facts.text: Krisha stars his aunt, Krisha Fairchild, and was shot in his mother's house.

davidrobertmitchell.signature: Dreamy suburban nightmares of teenage life.
davidrobertmitchell.description: His films set coming-of-age stories in timeless Michigan suburbs and in Los Angeles, borrowing the slow dread of John Carpenter.

facts.text: It Follows was shot in and around Detroit.

alexrossperry.signature: Abrasive literary comedies about unpleasant people.
alexrossperry.description: He shoots on 16mm with tight, handheld close-ups of characters whose wit and cruelty fill every scene.

facts.text: Listen Up Philip has novelistic narration read by Eric Bogosian.

andrewbujalski.description: His low-budget comedies of awkward young adults, shot with friends as actors, started the mumblecore wave.

facts.text: Computer Chess was shot on vintage black-and-white video cameras.

joeswanberg.signature: The most prolific improviser of mumblecore.
joeswanberg.description: He made a long run of cheap, improvised films about relationships, often with fellow filmmakers as actors.

facts.text: Hannah Takes the Stairs features Greta Gerwig, Mark Duplass and Andrew Bujalski as actors.

jaymarkduplass.signature: Brothers who took mumblecore from festivals to the studios.
jaymarkduplass.description: Their improvised comedies about awkward men and families use restless zooms and handheld camera.

facts.text: Their first feature, The Puffy Chair, premiered at Sundance in 2005.

elizahittman.signature: Intimate, near-silent films of teenagers on the edges of New York.
elizahittman.description: She films adolescent desire and danger in Brooklyn and on the road with close, grainy images and few words.

facts.text: Never Rarely Sometimes Always won the Grand Jury Prize at the Berlinale.

josephinedecker.signature: Delirious, sensory films about women's minds.
josephinedecker.description: Her films dissolve narrative into texture, with a camera that sways and lunges and soundtracks that unsettle.

facts.text: Shirley stars Elisabeth Moss as the writer Shirley Jackson.

kogonada.signature: A video essayist on Ozu who makes films of serene symmetry.
kogonada.description: He became known for video essays on Ozu, Bresson and Kubrick; his features frame people against modernist architecture.

facts.text: Columbus is set among the modernist buildings of Columbus, Indiana.

celinesong.description: A Korean-Canadian playwright whose debut film follows two childhood friends meeting again across decades and continents.

facts.text: Past Lives was nominated for the Best Picture Oscar.

boburnham.signature: A YouTube comedian turned chronicler of online life.
boburnham.description: He grew up performing online; his film and specials examine anxiety and performance in the internet age.

facts.text: Inside was written, shot and edited alone in one room during the 2020 lockdown.

deerees.signature: Dramas of Black lives, from Brooklyn to the Mississippi Delta.
deerees.description: Her films range from an autobiographical coming-out story to an epic of two families in the postwar Delta.

facts.text: Mudbound's Rachel Morrison was the first woman nominated for the cinematography Oscar.

avaduvernay.signature: Historical drama and documentary about race and justice in America.
avaduvernay.description: A former publicist whose films and series examine the civil rights movement and mass incarceration.

facts.text: Selma made her the first Black woman nominated for the Golden Globe for best director.
13th was nominated for the documentary Oscar.

bootsriley.signature: Surreal anti-capitalist satire from an Oakland rapper.
bootsriley.description: Frontman of the hip-hop group The Coup, he turned to film with a surreal comedy about telemarketing and labour.

facts.text: Fronts the hip-hop group The Coup.

ramellross.signature: Photographic attention to Black lives in the American South.
ramellross.description: A photographer and teacher in Alabama whose documentary is built from fragments rather than a story; his first fiction feature is shot entirely from its protagonists' points of view.

facts.text: Nickel Boys is filmed in first-person point of view.

abelferrara.signature: Catholic guilt and New York sleaze.
abelferrara.description: His crime and horror films follow addicts, killers and corrupt cops through New York, searching for grace.

facts.text: Zoë Lund, the star of Ms .45, co-wrote Bad Lieutenant.

paulschrader.signature: The critic of transcendental style who wrote Taxi Driver.
paulschrader.description: He wrote or co-wrote Taxi Driver, Raging Bull and The Last Temptation of Christ for Scorsese, and directs films about lonely men keeping diaries, often modelled on Bresson.

facts.text: Wrote the book Transcendental Style in Film, on Ozu, Bresson and Dreyer.

walterhill.description: A screenwriter and director of stripped-down westerns and urban action movies with minimal dialogue.

facts.text: The Warriors is loosely based on Xenophon's Anabasis, by way of Sol Yurick's novel.

joedante.signature: Subversive creature features soaked in cartoon and B-movie lore.
joedante.description: A Roger Corman graduate whose monster comedies satirise American suburbia, with cameos from old genre actors.

facts.text: Started out cutting trailers for Roger Corman's New World Pictures.

wescraven.description: A former humanities lecturer who made brutal exploitation horror, then the dream-killer Freddy Krueger, then the self-aware Scream.

facts.text: Taught humanities at university before turning to film.

mnightshyamalan.signature: Slow-burning suspense and the twist ending.
mnightshyamalan.description: Based in Philadelphia, he makes supernatural thrillers with quiet long takes and endings that reframe what came before.

facts.text: The Sixth Sense received six Oscar nominations.

mikemills.signature: A graphic designer's essays on parents and memory.
mikemills.description: A designer and music-video maker whose films about his own father and mother mix narration, photographs and archive images.

facts.text: Christopher Plummer won the supporting actor Oscar for Beginners, playing a character based on Mills's father.

panoscosmatos.description: His films soak 1980s genre imagery in red light and slow, heavy synthesiser scores.

facts.text: Is the son of the director George P. Cosmatos.

alexgarland.signature: A novelist turned director of cerebral science fiction.
alexgarland.description: He wrote The Beach and screenplays for Danny Boyle before directing films about artificial minds, mutation and civil war.

facts.text: Wrote the novel The Beach and the script of 28 Days Later.

benwheatley.signature: Folk horror, hitmen and chaos in the English countryside.
benwheatley.description: He came from viral videos and television comedy; his films mix kitchen-sink realism with occult horror and black comedy.

facts.text: A Field in England is set during the English Civil War and was shot in black and white.

peterstrickland.signature: Loving pastiches of European cult cinema.
peterstrickland.description: His films recreate the textures of 1970s giallo, Eurohorror and erotic cinema with fetishistic attention to sound and objects.

facts.text: Berberian Sound Studio is set in the sound studio of an Italian horror film.

markjenkin.description: A Cornish director who shoots on clockwork 16mm cameras, develops the film by hand and records all the sound afterwards.

facts.text: Bait was shot on a hand-wound Bolex camera and processed by hand.

shanemeadows.signature: Funny, violent stories of the English Midlands.
shanemeadows.description: He makes semi-autobiographical films about working-class youth in the Midlands with largely untrained casts.

facts.text: This Is England is based on his own adolescence in the early 1980s.

charlottewells.signature: A father-daughter holiday reassembled from memory and camcorder tape.
charlottewells.description: A Scottish director whose debut feature recalls a Turkish holiday through the gaps between home video and memory.

facts.text: Aftersun was her first feature.

lukasmoodysson.signature: Tender, rough films of Swedish teenagers and communes.
lukasmoodysson.description: A poet turned director whose early films about adolescents and a 1970s commune are shot with restless handheld zooms.

facts.text: Together is set in a Stockholm commune in 1975.

nicolaswindingrefn.description: He began with handheld Copenhagen crime films and moved to stylised, slow, colour-saturated thrillers with sparse dialogue.

facts.text: Won Best Director at Cannes for Drive.

hlynurpalmason.signature: Elemental Icelandic dramas of weather and time.
hlynurpalmason.description: His films observe people against the Icelandic landscape, often with time-lapse and long fixed shots.

facts.text: Godland follows a Danish priest travelling across 19th-century Iceland.

olivierassayas.signature: Restless, globetrotting films about art, commerce and ghosts.
olivierassayas.description: A former Cahiers du cinéma critic whose fluid camera follows characters through the fashion, film and art worlds, and through recent history.

facts.text: Was a critic at Cahiers du cinéma.
Carlos was made as a television miniseries of more than five hours.

miahansenlve.signature: Delicate films of time passing in ordinary lives.
miahansenlve.description: A former actress for Olivier Assayas, she makes elliptical films about grief, love and work that cross years in a few cuts.

facts.text: Things to Come won the Silver Bear for best director.

arnauddesplechin.description: His films are dense, digressive family novels full of quotations, flashbacks and direct address, often with Mathieu Amalric.

facts.text: Mathieu Amalric plays his recurring alter ego, Paul Dédalus.

brunodumont.signature: Mystical films of the French north, from austerity to slapstick.
brunodumont.description: A former philosophy teacher who casts local non-professionals in the Pas-de-Calais, moving from bleak spiritual dramas to grotesque comedy.

facts.text: L'Humanité won the Grand Prix at Cannes and both acting prizes, for two non-professionals.

alainguiraudie.signature: Desire and danger in the rural south of France.
alainguiraudie.description: His films treat sex and longing among working people in Occitanie with frankness, deadpan humour and suspense.

facts.text: Stranger by the Lake is set entirely at a cruising spot by a lake.

francoisozon.signature: A prolific chameleon of French cinema.
francoisozon.description: He makes roughly a film a year, moving between melodrama, musical, thriller and comedy, often with a provocative or queer edge.

facts.text: 8 Women brought together Catherine Deneuve, Isabelle Huppert, Fanny Ardant and Emmanuelle Béart.

philippegarrel.signature: Black-and-white chronicles of love after May '68.
philippegarrel.description: His autobiographical films about lovers, drugs and artistic life in Paris use long takes and few retakes, often with his family as actors.

facts.text: Was the singer Nico's partner for most of the 1970s; she appears in several of his films.
Regular Lovers won the Silver Lion at Venice.

catherinebreillat.description: A novelist turned director whose films examine desire, shame and power from young women's points of view.

facts.text: Published her first novel at 17.

robincampillo.signature: Group portraits of activists and outsiders.
robincampillo.description: A screenwriter and editor for Laurent Cantet whose own films capture collective life, most famously the AIDS activists of ACT UP Paris.

facts.text: BPM (Beats per Minute) draws on his own time in ACT UP Paris and won the Grand Prix at Cannes.
Co-wrote and edited Cantet's The Class.

alicediop.signature: A documentarian of France's suburbs and its courts.
alicediop.description: She made documentaries about the Paris banlieue before a fiction feature built from the transcripts of a real trial.

facts.text: Saint Omer won the Grand Jury Prize at Venice.

xavierdolan.signature: A Quebec prodigy of operatic family melodrama.
xavierdolan.description: He directed his first feature at 19 and makes emotionally excessive films about mothers and sons, with pop music and slow motion.

facts.text: Mommy is framed in a square 1:1 ratio that widens at moments of hope.

guymaddin.signature: A Winnipeg fantasist who makes new films that look like lost silent ones.
guymaddin.description: His films imitate the look of decaying early cinema, with iris shots, intertitles and melodrama, to tell feverish stories about family and memory.

facts.text: My Winnipeg is a 'docu-fantasia' about his home city.

christianpetzold.signature: Ghost stories of German history told as melodramas.
christianpetzold.description: The best-known director of the Berlin School, he reworks noir and melodrama to show people haunted by the GDR and the Second World War, often with Nina Hoss or Paula Beer.

facts.text: Barbara won the Silver Bear for best director.
Harun Farocki co-wrote several of his films.

valeskagrisebach.signature: Westerns of masculinity with non-professional casts.
valeskagrisebach.description: Associated with the Berlin School, she casts non-actors and builds her films slowly from their lives.

facts.text: Western follows German construction workers in rural Bulgaria.

ulrichseidl.signature: Frontal tableaux of Austrian loneliness and cruelty.
ulrichseidl.description: He stages people in fixed, symmetrical tableaux and blurs documentary and fiction, often provoking audiences with sex and humiliation.

facts.text: Made the Paradise trilogy: Love, Faith and Hope.

jessicahausner.signature: Cool, artificial colour and deadpan ambiguity.
jessicahausner.description: Her films frame people in stylised colour schemes and fixed shots, leaving miracles and motives unexplained.

facts.text: Lourdes was filmed at the pilgrimage site itself.

lukasdhont.signature: Tender, wrenching films of adolescent identity.
lukasdhont.description: A Belgian director whose films stay close to young protagonists' faces and bodies.

facts.text: Girl won the Caméra d'Or at Cannes and Close the Grand Prix.

alexanderkluge.signature: The theorist and collagist of the New German Cinema.
alexanderkluge.description: A lawyer and writer who drafted the Oberhausen Manifesto and made fragmentary essay films mixing fiction, documents and commentary.

facts.text: Was a principal author of the 1962 Oberhausen Manifesto.
Coordinated the collective film Germany in Autumn.

margarethevontrotta.signature: Political history told through women's lives.
margarethevontrotta.description: An actress turned director, she makes films about sisters, terrorists and intellectuals, often with Barbara Sukowa.

facts.text: Marianne and Juliane won the Golden Lion.

alekseibalabanov.description: His gangster films became cult classics of post-Soviet Russia, while his other films are bleak period pieces about cruelty.

facts.text: Brother is scored with songs by the rock band Nautilus Pompilius.

kantemirbalagov.signature: Harrowing postwar dramas in green and red.
kantemirbalagov.description: A student of Aleksandr Sokurov whose films about women after trauma are built on saturated colour and long close shots.

facts.text: Studied in Aleksandr Sokurov's workshop in Nalchik.

sergeiloznitsa.signature: Archival and observational films of mass history.
sergeiloznitsa.description: Raised in Kyiv, he alternates found-footage documentaries about Soviet and Nazi history with bleak fictions.

facts.text: State Funeral is built entirely from footage of Stalin's funeral.

kirillserebrennikov.signature: Theatrical bravura about artists and dissidents.
kirillserebrennikov.description: A stage director whose films fold music, fantasy and long takes into stories of Soviet rock, illness and exile.

facts.text: Leto is about the Leningrad rock scene of the early 1980s.

radujude.signature: Rude, essayistic satire of Romanian history.
radujude.description: He moved from realist dramas to collage and essay films that confront Romania's history of slavery and its part in the Holocaust.

facts.text: Bad Luck Banging or Loony Porn won the Golden Bear.

corneliuporumboiu.signature: Deadpan comedies about language and meaning.
corneliuporumboiu.description: His films turn arguments over words, definitions and evidence into dry comedy.

facts.text: 12:08 East of Bucharest won the Caméra d'Or at Cannes.

agnieszkaholland.signature: A Polish director of moral anxiety and modern history.
agnieszkaholland.description: She worked with Andrzej Wajda in Poland's cinema of moral anxiety, then made films abroad about the Holocaust, totalitarianism and Europe's borders.

facts.text: Europa Europa was nominated for the adapted screenplay Oscar.
Green Border won the Special Jury Prize at Venice.

krzysztofzanussi.signature: A physicist's cinema of moral and intellectual dilemmas.
krzysztofzanussi.description: Trained in physics and philosophy, he made cerebral dramas central to Poland's cinema of moral anxiety.

facts.text: Illumination follows a physicist's life, with documentary inserts.

otariosseliani.signature: Wry, wandering comedies of idlers, from Tbilisi to Paris.
otariosseliani.description: A Georgian musician turned filmmaker whose gentle, nearly wordless comedies drift between many characters.

facts.text: Moved to France in 1982 and made most of his later films there.

tengizabuladze.signature: Made the allegory that broke the Soviet silence about the terror.
tengizabuladze.description: His trilogy of Georgian parables ended with Repentance, a grotesque satire of a Stalin-like dictator released during glasnost.

facts.text: Repentance won the Grand Prix at Cannes in 1987.

athinaracheltsangari.signature: A founder of the Greek Weird Wave.
athinaracheltsangari.description: A producer of the movement's early films whose own work stages strange, awkward behaviour with deadpan humour.

facts.text: Yorgos Lanthimos acts in her film Attenberg.

albertserra.signature: Languid, decadent tableaux of historical figures.
albertserra.description: A Catalan provocateur whose films about Don Quixote, the Magi, Casanova and Louis XIV are made of long, improvised takes.

facts.text: The Death of Louis XIV stars Jean-Pierre Léaud.

mariobava.signature: The father of Italian Gothic horror and the giallo.
mariobava.description: A former cinematographer who painted his horror films in saturated colour and shadow on tiny budgets.

facts.text: Blood and Black Lace is often cited as a model for both the giallo and the slasher film.

matteogarrone.signature: Fairy tales and crime stories from Italy's margins.
matteogarrone.description: A former painter whose films range from the Camorra epic Gomorrah to fables and folk tales.

facts.text: Gomorrah won the Grand Prix at Cannes.

lisandroalonso.signature: Wordless journeys of solitary men through remote landscapes.
lisandroalonso.description: His films follow non-professional loners working and wandering in jungle, forest and pampas, in very long takes.

facts.text: Jauja stars Viggo Mortensen and is framed in a nearly square ratio with rounded corners.

matiaspineiro.signature: Playful variations on Shakespeare among young Argentine women.
matiaspineiro.description: His films, mostly set among young actresses rehearsing and gossiping in Buenos Aires, riff on Shakespeare's comedies.

facts.text: Several of his films are named after Shakespeare heroines, such as Rosalinda and Viola.

klebermendoncafilho.signature: A critic's portraits of Recife, between social drama and genre film.
klebermendoncafilho.description: A former critic whose films about the city of Recife study class, property and memory, sometimes erupting into violence.

facts.text: Bacurau, co-directed with Juliano Dornelles, won the Jury Prize at Cannes.
Won Best Director at Cannes for The Secret Agent in 2025.

pablolarrain.signature: Dark portraits of Chile under Pinochet, and of icons in crisis.
pablolarrain.description: His films about the Pinochet era are grim and absurd; later he made portraits of famous women at breaking point.

facts.text: No was shot on vintage U-matic video cameras to blend with 1988 archive footage.

ciroguerra.description: His films about Amazonian and Wayuu communities, several co-directed with Cristina Gallego, mix ethnography with epic.

facts.text: Embrace of the Serpent was the first Colombian film nominated for the foreign-language Oscar.

amatescalante.signature: Shocking, deadpan violence in contemporary Mexico.
amatescalante.description: He films brutal stories of poverty and cartel violence in fixed, patient shots.

facts.text: Won Best Director at Cannes for Heli.

diaoyinan.signature: Chinese film noir in neon and snow.
diaoyinan.description: A playwright turned director whose crime films set noir plots in the grubby underworld of provincial Chinese cities.

facts.text: Black Coal, Thin Ice won the Golden Bear.

louye.signature: Passionate, handheld films of desire, banned more than once.
louye.description: His sensual, fragmentary love stories have repeatedly run into Chinese censorship.

facts.text: Was banned from filmmaking for five years after showing Summer Palace at Cannes without approval.

johnnieto.signature: Hong Kong's master of geometric gunfights and gangster ritual.
johnnieto.description: Through his company Milkyway Image he made precisely choreographed crime films about loyalty and fate.

facts.text: Co-founded the production company Milkyway Image in 1996.

annhui.signature: A humane chronicler of Hong Kong and its people.
annhui.description: A leading figure of the Hong Kong New Wave of 1979, she has made social dramas, literary adaptations and stories of migrants and the elderly for four decades.

facts.text: Received the Golden Lion for lifetime achievement in 2020.
A Simple Life won Deanie Ip the best actress prize at Venice.

stanleykwan.signature: Melancholy melodramas of memory and desire.
stanleykwan.description: A former assistant to Ann Hui, he made elegant films about women and about queer Hong Kong.

facts.text: Center Stage mixes a biopic of the actress Ruan Lingyu with interviews and archive footage.

nahongjin.signature: Relentless Korean thrillers that turn into horror.
nahongjin.description: His films start as police or chase thrillers and end in exhausting, ambiguous violence and the supernatural.

facts.text: The Wailing mixes a police procedural with shamanism.

kimjeewoon.signature: A stylist who has made a film in almost every genre.
kimjeewoon.description: His films move between horror, gangster film, western and spy thriller, each staged with polish and dark humour.

facts.text: The Good, the Bad, the Weird is a tribute to Sergio Leone set in 1930s Manchuria.

naomikawase.signature: Lyrical films of Nara's forests, family and death.
naomikawase.description: She began with diary documentaries about her own family and makes fiction films with the same intimate, nature-filled camera.

facts.text: Won the Caméra d'Or at Cannes for Suzaku and the Grand Prix for The Mourning Forest.

takashimiike.signature: Japan's most prolific and outrageous genre director.
takashimiike.description: He has made more than a hundred films, from direct-to-video yakuza films to period epics, notorious for extreme violence and absurdity.

facts.text: Worked as an assistant director for Shohei Imamura.

sionsono.signature: Excessive, anarchic films of faith and family.
sionsono.description: A poet turned director whose long, wild films mix religion, voyeurism, violence and melodrama.

facts.text: Love Exposure runs nearly four hours.

shunjiiwai.signature: Bittersweet youth films in soft, overexposed light.
shunjiiwai.description: A music-video director whose films about adolescence and memory use bleached colour and a drifting handheld camera.

facts.text: All About Lily Chou-Chou is partly told through messages on an internet fan forum.

shinjisomai.signature: A master of the extremely long take.
shinjisomai.description: His films about teenagers and families are built from long, often single-shot scenes that push his young actors hard.

facts.text: Typhoon Club follows students trapped in their school during a typhoon.

nobuhikoobayashi.signature: Psychedelic, handmade fantasies from a former commercials director.
nobuhikoobayashi.description: He made experimental shorts and television commercials before his debut House, and late in life a series of collage-like anti-war films.

facts.text: House was partly based on ideas from his young daughter.

mamoruoshii.signature: Philosophical anime of cities, dogs and machines.
mamoruoshii.description: His animated films slow down for long, contemplative city sequences and debates about identity and reality.

facts.text: Ghost in the Shell is often cited as an influence on The Matrix.

masaakiyuasa.description: His films and series stretch bodies and perspective with free, sketchy drawing and a manic pace.

facts.text: Directed the series The Tatami Galaxy and Devilman Crybaby.

makotoshinkai.description: He began by animating a short almost entirely alone on his computer; his features are melancholy romances under luminous skies.

facts.text: Your Name. became one of the highest-grossing anime films ever.

mamoruhosoda.signature: Family adventures across real and virtual worlds.
mamoruhosoda.description: His animated films alternate between digital worlds and rural Japan to tell stories of families and growing up.

facts.text: Mirai was nominated for the Oscar for animated feature.

maniratnam.signature: Tamil cinema's great stylist of romance and politics.
maniratnam.description: His films set love stories against riots, terrorism and war, with songs by A. R. Rahman and lush camera work.

facts.text: Roja was A. R. Rahman's first film score.

mrinalsen.signature: The political modernist of Bengali cinema.
mrinalsen.description: Alongside Satyajit Ray and Ritwik Ghatak, he made Bengali cinema's most overtly political and formally playful films.

facts.text: Bhuvan Shome is often cited as the start of India's New Cinema.

shyambenegal.signature: The founder of Hindi parallel cinema's realist strand.
shyambenegal.description: A former advertising filmmaker whose rural dramas of caste and exploitation launched a generation of actors.

facts.text: Manthan was financed by some 500,000 dairy farmers, each contributing two rupees.

adoorgopalakrishnan.signature: Kerala's master of quiet, precise films about decline.
adoorgopalakrishnan.description: A pioneer of Malayalam art cinema whose films study feudal decline and inner life with restraint.

facts.text: Elippathayam won the British Film Institute's Sutherland Trophy.

payalkapadia.signature: Dreamlike films of women in Mumbai.
payalkapadia.description: Her films blend documentary and fiction, letters and night-time city scenes.

facts.text: All We Imagine as Light won the Grand Prix at Cannes, the first Indian film in the main competition there in 30 years.

chaitanyatamhane.signature: Patient, observational dramas of Mumbai's institutions.
chaitanyatamhane.description: He films courtrooms and music lessons in long, static wide shots, letting the system reveal itself.

facts.text: The Disciple won the screenplay prize at Venice.

majidmajidi.signature: Tender films of children and faith.
majidmajidi.description: His simple, emotional stories about poor children and families found audiences around the world.

facts.text: Children of Heaven was the first Iranian film nominated for the foreign-language Oscar.

mohammadrasoulof.signature: Dissident parables of complicity under the Islamic Republic.
mohammadrasoulof.description: Repeatedly banned from filmmaking, he makes films clandestinely about ordinary people forced into moral compromise.

facts.text: There Is No Evil won the Golden Bear.
Left Iran in 2024 before the premiere of The Seed of the Sacred Fig at Cannes.

nadinelabaki.signature: Lebanese ensemble comedies and street-level melodramas.
nadinelabaki.description: An actress-director whose films cast non-professionals to tell stories of Beirut's women and children.

facts.text: Capernaum won the Jury Prize at Cannes.

kaoutherbenhania.signature: Hybrids of documentary and re-enactment from Tunisia.
kaoutherbenhania.description: Her films question how stories are told, staging real people alongside actors.

facts.text: In Four Daughters, members of a real family play themselves alongside actresses.

mahamatsalehharoun.signature: Austere fables of fathers and sons in Chad.
mahamatsalehharoun.description: The leading director of Chad, he makes spare dramas about war, revenge and family.

facts.text: A Screaming Man won the Jury Prize at Cannes.

alaingomis.description: A French-Senegalese director whose films follow characters through Dakar and Kinshasa, with music at their centre.

facts.text: Félicité won the Grand Jury Prize at the Berlinale.

hailegerima.signature: The L.A. Rebellion's fiercest political voice.
hailegerima.description: An Ethiopian-born director who studied at UCLA and made radical films about Black life in Los Angeles, about slavery and about Ethiopia.

facts.text: Distributed Sankofa himself after the industry passed on it.

rithypanh.signature: Documents the Khmer Rouge genocide that he survived.
rithypanh.description: A survivor of the Khmer Rouge labour camps, he makes documentaries that confront perpetrators and reconstruct memory.

facts.text: The Missing Picture uses clay figurines to show what no footage recorded.

brillantemendoza.description: He films poverty, crime and survival in the Philippines in a raw, handheld style.

facts.text: Won Best Director at Cannes for Kinatay.

taikawaititi.description: He moved from small comedies about awkward children and vampire flatmates to superhero blockbusters.

facts.text: Won the adapted screenplay Oscar for Jojo Rabbit.

warwickthornton.signature: Aboriginal stories from Central Australia, shot by the director himself.
warwickthornton.description: A cinematographer and director from Alice Springs who films Aboriginal lives with few words and vast landscapes.

facts.text: Samson and Delilah won the Caméra d'Or at Cannes.

aliceguyblache.signature: The first woman director, and one of the first to tell stories on film.
aliceguyblache.description: Secretary to Léon Gaumont, she began directing narrative films for his company in 1896, ran its production for a decade, then founded her own studio, Solax, in the United States.

facts.text: Made some of the first films with synchronised sound, using Gaumont's Chronophone.
Founded the Solax studio in Fort Lee, New Jersey, in 1910.

edwinsporter.signature: Edison's director, who built The Great Train Robbery from separate shots.
edwinsporter.description: A projectionist who became Thomas Edison's leading film-maker, he assembled stories from shots taken in different places and times, an early basis of film editing.

facts.text: The Great Train Robbery ends with a bandit firing straight at the audience.
Life of an American Fireman combines staged scenes with footage of real fire crews.

maxlinder.signature: The dapper star of early French film comedy, a model for Chaplin.
maxlinder.description: Pathé's biggest star before the First World War, he wrote and directed comedies about his elegant, unlucky man-about-town, and later made features in Hollywood.

facts.text: Seven Years Bad Luck contains the mirror routine later used by the Marx Brothers in Duck Soup.
The Three Must-Get-Theres parodies Douglas Fairbanks's The Three Musketeers.

macksennett.signature: The 'King of Comedy' whose Keystone studio made slapstick an industry.
macksennett.description: A former Griffith actor who founded Keystone in 1912, producing and often directing chaotic chase comedies with the Keystone Cops and giving Chaplin his start in film.

facts.text: Chaplin made his first films at Keystone in 1914.
Received an honorary Oscar for his contribution to screen comedy.

thomashince.signature: The producer who organised film-making around the shooting script.
thomashince.description: A director turned producer who built Inceville, a studio ranch near Santa Monica, and ran production from detailed continuity scripts, a model for the Hollywood studio system.

facts.text: Co-directed the anti-war epic Civilization.

allandwan.signature: A director of some 400 films, from the earliest Westerns to 1950s Technicolor.
allandwan.description: An engineer who drifted into films in 1909, he directed Douglas Fairbanks's Robin Hood and Gloria Swanson's comedies, then Shirley Temple films and lean, colourful B-films.

facts.text: Often credited with the first dolly shot, putting the camera on a moving car for David Harum in 1915.
Sands of Iwo Jima earned John Wayne his first Oscar nomination.

rexingram.signature: The painterly director who made Valentino a star.
rexingram.description: An Irish-born sculptor turned director whose lavish, pictorial epics of the early 1920s were among the biggest hits of the silent era; he later ran his own studio in Nice.

facts.text: The Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse was one of the highest-grossing silent films.
Michael Powell began his career at Ingram's studio in Nice.

germainedulac.signature: A pioneer of French impressionist and surrealist film, and a feminist critic.
germainedulac.description: A journalist and feminist who became a leading figure of the French avant-garde in the 1920s, writing about 'pure cinema' and making films that render a character's inner life in images.

facts.text: The Seashell and the Clergyman, from a scenario by Antonin Artaud, is often called the first surrealist film.
The Smiling Madame Beudet shows a wife's fantasies of escaping her marriage.

marcellherbier.signature: The aesthete of French impressionism, who built films like modernist exhibitions.
marcellherbier.description: A poet and dramatist who made stylised films with leading architects and painters, and later founded IDHEC, the French national film school.

facts.text: L'Inhumaine has sets by the architect Robert Mallet-Stevens and the painter Fernand Léger.
Founded the film school IDHEC in 1943.

jacquesfeyder.signature: The Belgian director of Carnival in Flanders and teacher of Marcel Carné.
jacquesfeyder.description: Working in France, Hollywood and Britain, he made polished literary adaptations and satires, and his realism shaped the poetic realist films of his assistant Marcel Carné.

facts.text: Directed Greta Garbo in The Kiss, often called MGM's last silent film.
Marcel Carné was his assistant on several films.

paulleni.signature: A set designer whose expressionist style carried into Hollywood horror.
paulleni.description: A painter and set designer who directed the expressionist anthology Waxworks, then moved to Universal, where his shadowy, angular style shaped the studio's horror films.

facts.text: Conrad Veidt's grin in The Man Who Laughs inspired the look of Batman's Joker.
The Cat and the Canary set the pattern of the haunted-house film.

paulwegener.signature: The actor-director who brought the Golem to the screen.
paulwegener.description: A leading actor of Max Reinhardt's company who saw film as a medium for the fantastic, he co-directed and starred in The Student of Prague and three films about the Golem of Jewish legend.

facts.text: Plays the clay giant in The Golem: How He Came into the World, co-directed with Carl Boese.

eadupont.signature: Directed Variety, whose swinging camera dazzled Hollywood.
eadupont.description: A film critic turned director whose circus melodrama Variety, shot by Karl Freund with a camera that flies with the trapeze artists, led to work in Britain and Hollywood.

facts.text: Made Piccadilly in London with Anna May Wong.

arnoldfanck.signature: Inventor of the German mountain film.
arnoldfanck.description: A geologist who filmed skiers and climbers on real peaks and built melodramas around the danger of the Alps; Leni Riefenstahl started as his actress.

facts.text: Co-directed The White Hell of Pitz Palu with G. W. Pabst.
Leni Riefenstahl acted in several of his films before she directed.

hansrichter.signature: A Dada artist who made some of the first abstract films.
hansrichter.description: A painter of the Dada movement who animated geometric shapes in his Rhythmus films of the early 1920s, then taught in New York and made Dreams That Money Can Buy with Duchamp, Ernst, Léger and Man Ray.

facts.text: Rhythmus 21 is among the first abstract films.

mauritzstiller.signature: The Swedish director who discovered Greta Garbo.
mauritzstiller.description: With Victor Sjöström he led the golden age of Swedish silent film, moving between sophisticated comedies and literary sagas, and took Garbo with him to Hollywood.

facts.text: Cast Garbo in The Saga of Gösta Berling and brought her to MGM.
Erotikon is often named as an influence on Ernst Lubitsch's sex comedies.

benjaminchristensen.signature: Director of Häxan, a silent essay film on witchcraft.
benjaminchristensen.description: A Danish actor and director whose Häxan mixes lecture, engravings and staged scenes of devils and witches, before he worked in Hollywood on horror films.

facts.text: Plays the Devil in Häxan.

yakovprotazanov.signature: The most popular film-maker of tsarist Russia, who returned to make Aelita.
yakovprotazanov.description: He directed literary adaptations before the revolution, emigrated, then came back in 1923 to make the science-fiction film Aelita, with constructivist sets, followed by popular comedies.

facts.text: Aelita: Queen of Mars has costumes by the constructivist artist Aleksandra Ekster.

levkuleshov.signature: The teacher whose experiments gave montage its first theory.
levkuleshov.description: At the state film school he ran a workshop that tested how editing creates meaning, the 'Kuleshov effect', and taught Pudovkin and Barnet, while directing satires and a Western.

facts.text: The Extraordinary Adventures of Mr. West in the Land of the Bolsheviks satirises American ideas about Soviet Russia.
By the Law adapts a Jack London story.

vsevolodpudovkin.signature: The montage director who told the revolution through a mother's awakening.
vsevolodpudovkin.description: A chemist turned film-maker trained by Kuleshov, he linked shots into an emotional chain and told history through individual characters, and wrote influential books on film technique.

facts.text: Mother is adapted from Maxim Gorky's novel.
Signed the 1928 statement on sound film with Eisenstein and Grigori Alexandrov.

grigorikozintsev.signature: Co-founder of the Factory of the Eccentric Actor, later the director of a great Soviet Hamlet.
grigorikozintsev.description: With Leonid Trauberg he founded FEKS in Petrograd in 1921 and made grotesque, eccentric silents and the Maxim trilogy, then alone filmed Shakespeare with music by Shostakovich.

facts.text: His Hamlet and King Lear use Boris Pasternak's translations and scores by Dmitri Shostakovich.

abramroom.signature: Director of Bed and Sofa, a frank silent comedy of a Moscow ménage à trois.
abramroom.description: A doctor turned director whose intimate films about everyday Soviet life, shot partly on the streets of Moscow, stood apart from the epics of montage.

facts.text: A Strict Young Man was banned in 1936 and not shown for decades.

esfirshub.signature: Invented the compilation film from old newsreels.
esfirshub.description: An editor who recut imported films for Soviet audiences, she assembled The Fall of the Romanov Dynasty from tsarist newsreels and home movies, founding the archive documentary.

facts.text: Searched archives and private collections for footage of the tsar's family for The Fall of the Romanov Dynasty.

johngrierson.signature: Founder of the British documentary movement, who gave 'documentary' its meaning.
johngrierson.description: A Scottish producer who set up film units at the Empire Marketing Board, the GPO and the National Film Board of Canada, directing only Drifters himself and training a generation of film-makers.

facts.text: First used the word 'documentary' for a film in a 1926 review of Robert Flaherty's Moana.
Founded the National Film Board of Canada in 1939.

winsormccay.signature: The comic-strip artist who made animation an art.
winsormccay.description: Creator of the strip Little Nemo in Slumberland, he drew thousands of frames by hand for Gertie the Dinosaur and The Sinking of the Lusitania, giving characters weight and personality.

facts.text: Performed live on the vaudeville stage alongside Gertie the Dinosaur, giving her commands.

ladislasstarevich.signature: Pioneer of stop-motion puppet film, starting with real insects.
ladislasstarevich.description: An entomologist who animated preserved beetles in Russia, then in France made intricate puppet films, including the feature The Tale of the Fox.

facts.text: The Cameraman's Revenge tells a tale of marital infidelity with animated beetles.

fleischerbrothers.signature: The New York rivals of Disney, behind Betty Boop and Popeye.
fleischerbrothers.description: Max invented the rotoscope and ran the studio, Dave directed: their surreal, jazz-scored cartoons of Koko the Clown, Betty Boop and Popeye were looser and stranger than Disney's.

facts.text: Snow-White rotoscopes Cab Calloway's dance moves for Koko singing St. James Infirmary Blues.
Made the animated features Gulliver's Travels and Mr. Bug Goes to Town.

texavery.signature: The cartoon director of speed, wild takes and broken rules.
texavery.description: At Warner Bros. he shaped Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, and at MGM made frantic cartoons that stretch bodies to extremes and talk to the audience across the frame.

facts.text: A Wild Hare is counted as the first Bugs Bunny cartoon, with the first 'What's up, Doc?'.

oskarfischinger.signature: The master of abstract animation set to music.
oskarfischinger.description: In Berlin he animated wax, paper and paint into visual music, then in Hollywood worked briefly on Disney's Fantasia, whose abstract opening draws on his ideas.

facts.text: Left Fantasia before its release; the Toccata and Fugue sequence keeps traces of his designs.
An Optical Poem was released by MGM in 1938.

jiritrnka.signature: The master of the puppet film, called the 'Walt Disney of the East'.
jiritrnka.description: A painter and illustrator who made Czech stop-motion puppet features into a national art, from folk tales to A Midsummer Night's Dream, with fixed faces that light alone makes expressive.

facts.text: His last film, The Hand, was read as an allegory of state control over the artist and was withdrawn after his death.

karelzeman.signature: Brought Jules Verne's engravings to life.
karelzeman.description: He combined live actors with animation, puppets and painted backdrops styled like 19th-century engravings, making fantastic voyages after Jules Verne and Baron Munchausen.

facts.text: Invention for Destruction recreates the look of the original illustrations of Verne's novels.

jansvankmajer.signature: The Czech surrealist of stop-motion, food, flesh and childhood fears.
jansvankmajer.description: A member of the Czech surrealist group who animates objects, meat and clay in tactile, grotesque close-ups, from Dimensions of Dialogue to his feature version of Alice.

facts.text: Dimensions of Dialogue shows clay heads devouring and regurgitating one another.

bradbird.signature: The Pixar director who brought the action film into animation.
bradbird.description: Trained by Disney veterans, he directed The Iron Giant at Warner Bros., then The Incredibles and Ratatouille at Pixar, before moving to live action.

facts.text: The Incredibles and Ratatouille each won the Oscar for Best Animated Feature.

harrysmith.signature: Folklorist, occultist and maker of hand-painted abstract films.
harrysmith.description: The compiler of the Anthology of American Folk Music also painted directly on film and made Heaven and Earth Magic, a cut-out animation of Victorian engravings.

facts.text: His Anthology of American Folk Music shaped the folk revival of the 1960s.

peterkubelka.description: An Austrian film-maker who composes very short films from single frames, as in Arnulf Rainer, and co-founded the Austrian Film Museum and Anthology Film Archives in New York.

facts.text: Arnulf Rainer consists only of black frames, white frames, white noise and silence.

kenjacobs.signature: Pulled a 1905 short apart, frame by frame, in Tom, Tom, the Piper's Son.
kenjacobs.description: A New York artist who reworks found footage to study perception, re-filming early cinema in close detail and later creating 3D effects in his Nervous System performances.

facts.text: Tom, Tom, the Piper's Son re-films a 1905 Biograph short to examine its every detail.

jamesbenning.signature: Films American landscapes in long, fixed shots.
jamesbenning.description: A former mathematics teacher who records rural and industrial America in long static takes, letting light, sound and passing traffic become the subject.

facts.text: 13 Lakes holds each of thirteen lakes for about ten minutes.
RR is made of shots of freight trains passing through the frame.

sufriedrich.signature: Personal essay films about family, faith and lesbian identity.
sufriedrich.description: An American experimental film-maker who works with text on screen, found footage and her own family history, as in Sink or Swim, about her father, told in 26 sections, one for each letter of the alphabet.

facts.text: Damned If You Don't sets a nun's desire against scenes from Black Narcissus.

marcobellocchio.signature: Italian cinema's lifelong rebel against family, church and state.
marcobellocchio.description: His debut Fists in the Pocket, about an epileptic young man who sets out to kill his family, made him a figure of 1960s revolt; later films revisit Italian history, from Mussolini to the Moro kidnapping.

facts.text: Received an honorary Palme d'Or at Cannes in 2021.

lilianacavani.signature: Director of The Night Porter, and of Francis of Assisi three times over.
lilianacavani.description: She began with historical documentaries for Italian television, then made provocative films about power, faith and sexuality, returning to Francis of Assisi across five decades.

facts.text: The Night Porter stars Dirk Bogarde and Charlotte Rampling as a former SS officer and a camp survivor who resume their relationship.

valeriozurlini.signature: A melancholic stylist of doomed love and waiting.
valeriozurlini.description: A director of restrained, elegiac films, from Family Diary with Marcello Mastroianni to The Desert of the Tartars, about soldiers waiting for an enemy who never comes.

facts.text: Family Diary shared the Golden Lion at Venice in 1962 with Tarkovsky's Ivan's Childhood.

luigicomencini.signature: The commedia all'italiana director most attuned to children.
luigicomencini.description: He moved from neorealist-tinged comedies such as Bread, Love and Dreams to social satire, and returned often to childhood, from Misunderstood to a celebrated television Pinocchio.

facts.text: Co-founded the Cineteca Italiana film archive in Milan.

vittoriodeseta.signature: Filmed the vanishing work of Sicilian and Sardinian peasants and fishermen.
vittoriodeseta.description: His short documentaries of the 1950s, in colour and widescreen and without commentary, record tuna fishing, sulphur mining and harvests in the south; his feature Bandits of Orgosolo was cast with Sardinian shepherds.

facts.text: Bandits of Orgosolo won the prize for best first film at Venice in 1961.

albertolattuada.signature: An eclectic stylist who co-directed Fellini's first film.
albertolattuada.description: A cultured, versatile director of literary adaptations and neorealist dramas, he co-directed Variety Lights with Federico Fellini and later made sensual comedies.

facts.text: Co-founded the Cineteca Italiana in Milan with Luigi Comencini.

julienduvivier.signature: The craftsman of poetic realism behind Pépé le Moko.
julienduvivier.description: A prolific director of fatalistic dramas in the 1930s, notably Pépé le Moko with Jean Gabin in the Casbah of Algiers, who worked in Hollywood during the war and later made the Don Camillo comedies.

facts.text: Pépé le Moko was remade in Hollywood as Algiers.

sachaguitry.signature: The playwright who narrated his films and played everyone's favourite cad.
sachaguitry.description: The most celebrated French dramatist of his day turned his wit to film, inventing playful narrated forms, as in The Story of a Cheat, told in his own voice over the images.

facts.text: The Story of a Cheat has almost no synchronised dialogue: Guitry narrates over the images.

claudesautet.signature: Chronicler of French middle-class friendships and love.
claudesautet.description: He made ensemble films around cafés and dinners with Yves Montand, Romy Schneider and Michel Piccoli, then late films of great restraint, Un cœur en hiver and Nelly and Monsieur Arnaud.

facts.text: Un cœur en hiver is set among string players and scored with Ravel.

bertrandtavernier.signature: A cinephile director and historian across genres, from crime to jazz.
bertrandtavernier.description: A critic and press agent turned director, he made period films, crime dramas and Round Midnight, about an American jazz musician in Paris, and wrote widely on American cinema.

facts.text: Round Midnight won the Oscar for Best Original Score for Herbie Hancock.
Worked as press agent on Jean-Pierre Melville's films.

andretechine.signature: A lyrical director of desire and youth in the French southwest.
andretechine.description: A former Cahiers critic whose films move between eras and lovers with restless camerawork, as in Wild Reeds, about boarding-school friends during the Algerian war.

facts.text: Wild Reeds won the César for Best Film.

pierreetaix.signature: Tati's collaborator who revived silent burlesque in the 1960s.
pierreetaix.description: A clown and gag writer who worked on Mon Oncle, then directed his own melancholy comedies full of sound gags; they were long unseen because of a rights dispute until their restoration in 2010.

facts.text: Won the Oscar for Best Live Action Short Film for Happy Anniversary, co-directed with Jean-Claude Carrière.

jacquesrozier.signature: The free-spirited outsider of the New Wave, of holidays by the sea.
jacquesrozier.description: His Adieu Philippine, about a young man awaiting military service in Algeria who flirts with two girls on holiday in Corsica, captured the New Wave's spontaneity; he made few, loose, improvised films after it.

facts.text: Les Naufragés de l'île de la Tortue stars Pierre Richard as a travel agent selling do-it-yourself Robinson Crusoe holidays.

bertrandblier.signature: Provocative, absurd comedies of male desire.
bertrandblier.description: The son of the actor Bernard Blier, he made Going Places with Gérard Depardieu and Patrick Dewaere, then increasingly surreal farces about couples and conventions.

facts.text: Get Out Your Handkerchiefs won the Oscar for Best Foreign Language Film.

jeanjacquesbeineix.signature: Launched the glossy 'cinéma du look' with Diva.
jeanjacquesbeineix.description: His Diva, a thriller about an opera fan and a bootleg recording, defined a stylish French cinema of colour and surface in the 1980s, followed by the passionate Betty Blue.

facts.text: Diva won the César for Best First Feature.

konradwolf.signature: The leading director of East German cinema.
konradwolf.description: Raised in exile in Moscow, he returned with the Red Army in 1945, as he recounts in I Was Nineteen, and became DEFA's most respected director and president of the East German Academy of Arts.

facts.text: Stars won the Special Jury Prize at Cannes in 1959.

frankbeyer.signature: DEFA director of Jacob the Liar and the banned Trace of Stones.
frankbeyer.description: His Trace of Stones, about a defiant construction foreman, was withdrawn days after its release in 1966; later Jacob the Liar became the only East German film nominated for an Oscar.

facts.text: Jacob the Liar was nominated for the Oscar for Best Foreign Language Film.

wolfgangstaudte.signature: Made the first German feature after the war, among the ruins of Berlin.
wolfgangstaudte.description: His The Murderers Are Among Us, shot in bombed Berlin for the new DEFA studio, confronts a doctor's guilt; he worked in both German states and satirised obedience to authority in The Kaiser's Lackey.

facts.text: The Murderers Are Among Us was the first German feature made after the Second World War.

helmutkautner.signature: A poetic stylist who kept his distance from Nazi propaganda while working inside the industry.
helmutkautner.description: A cabaret writer turned director whose wartime films, such as Romance in a Minor Key and Under the Bridges, tell quiet, lyrical stories, and who later made The Devil's General.

facts.text: Under the Bridges was shot in Berlin in 1944 and released after the war.

wernerschroeter.signature: The operatic extremist of New German Cinema.
wernerschroeter.description: Devoted to opera and to Maria Callas, he made stylised, ecstatic films of grand emotion, admired by Fassbinder, from Eika Katappa to The Kingdom of Naples.

facts.text: The Rose King was his last film with Magdalena Montezuma, made as she was dying.

rosavonpraunheim.signature: His 1971 film launched the West German gay rights movement.
rosavonpraunheim.description: A provocateur of queer cinema whose It Is Not the Homosexual Who Is Perverse, But the Society in Which He Lives sparked activist groups after its screenings, followed by decades of documentaries and camp melodramas.

facts.text: Gay activist groups formed across West Germany after screenings of his 1971 film.

helmasandersbrahms.signature: Told the war through her mother's eyes in Germany, Pale Mother.
helmasandersbrahms.description: A leading woman director of New German Cinema whose Germany, Pale Mother follows a mother and daughter through the bombing and the hungry postwar years, narrated by the director herself.

facts.text: Her daughter Anna plays the child in Germany, Pale Mother.

tonyrichardson.signature: Brought the Angry Young Men from the stage to the screen.
tonyrichardson.description: A founder of Free Cinema who directed Look Back in Anger on stage and screen, he shot northern working-class life on location, then won Oscars with the bawdy period romp Tom Jones.

facts.text: Tom Jones won the Oscars for Best Picture and Best Director.
Co-founded the production company Woodfall Films with John Osborne.

anthonyasquith.signature: The prime minister's son who filmed Shaw, Wilde and Rattigan.
anthonyasquith.description: Son of H. H. Asquith, he made the expressive silent Underground, then polished adaptations of Shaw, Wilde and Terence Rattigan, including Pygmalion and The Importance of Being Earnest.

facts.text: Co-directed Pygmalion with its star Leslie Howard.

thorolddickinson.signature: A precise stylist of British gothic, and of the first British film-studies department.
thorolddickinson.description: His Gaslight was suppressed by MGM to make way for its own remake, and The Queen of Spades became a cult film; he later founded the first university film department in Britain, at the Slade.

facts.text: MGM bought the rights to his Gaslight and tried to destroy the prints before releasing George Cukor's version.

basildearden.description: With the producer Michael Relph he made polished dramas and thrillers about race, crime and homosexuality, notably Victim, the first English-language film to use the word 'homosexual'.

facts.text: Victim, starring Dirk Bogarde, is credited with helping change British law on homosexuality.

charlescrichton.signature: Ealing comedy director who returned decades later for A Fish Called Wanda.
charlescrichton.description: An editor turned director of Ealing comedies, including The Lavender Hill Mob and The Titfield Thunderbolt, who after years in television co-wrote and directed A Fish Called Wanda with John Cleese.

facts.text: A Fish Called Wanda earned him Oscar nominations for Best Director and Best Original Screenplay.

juanantoniobardem.signature: A communist director who criticised Franco's Spain from inside it.
juanantoniobardem.description: With Luis García Berlanga he set out to renew Spanish cinema, making Death of a Cyclist and Main Street, stories of guilt and provincial hypocrisy; he was arrested during the shooting of the latter.

facts.text: Death of a Cyclist won the FIPRESCI Prize at Cannes in 1955.
His nephew is the actor Javier Bardem.

joseluisguerin.signature: A Catalan film-maker of looking, between documentary and fiction.
joseluisguerin.description: He makes quiet films that blur documentary and fiction, from Construction Site, about a building going up in Barcelona's Raval, to In the City of Sylvia, about a young man following a woman through Strasbourg.

facts.text: Construction Site won the Goya for Best Documentary.

joaocesarmonteiro.signature: Portuguese cinema's scandalous poet, playing his own lecherous alter ego.
joaocesarmonteiro.description: A critic and poet who cast himself as João de Deus, a gaunt, erudite libertine, in a trilogy of comic films of desire and literature, and ended with an almost black screen in Snow White.

facts.text: God's Comedy won the Grand Jury Prize at Venice in 1995.
His Snow White shows little but a dark screen.

paulorocha.signature: Opened the new Portuguese cinema with The Green Years.
paulorocha.description: After assisting Jean Renoir and Manoel de Oliveira, he made The Green Years, about a young shoemaker from the country lost in Lisbon, and later films drawn to Japan.

facts.text: Worked as Portugal's cultural attaché in Japan.

michaelcacoyannis.signature: Director of Zorba the Greek and of filmed Greek tragedy.
michaelcacoyannis.description: A Cypriot-born director who made Stella with Melina Mercouri, adapted Euripides with Irene Papas, and had his greatest success with Zorba the Greek.

facts.text: Zorba the Greek won three Oscars, including for Walter Lassally's cinematography.

metinerksan.signature: His Dry Summer won the Golden Bear for Turkey.
metinerksan.description: A central figure of Turkish cinema's golden age, he made Dry Summer, about a farmer who dams a stream to deny water to his neighbours, and Time to Love, a mystical romance.

facts.text: Dry Summer won the Golden Bear at Berlin in 1964.

omerkavur.signature: A Turkish modernist of solitude and obsession.
omerkavur.description: Trained in Paris, he made introspective films of loneliness and enigmatic journeys, such as Motherland Hotel, about a provincial hotel clerk, and The Secret Face.

facts.text: The Secret Face was written by Orhan Pamuk.

susannebier.signature: Danish director of family melodramas, from Dogme to international drama.
susannebier.description: She made Open Hearts under the Dogme rules, then glossier international dramas and the television series The Night Manager.

facts.text: In a Better World won the Oscar for Best Foreign Language Film.

caichusheng.signature: The left-wing melodramatist of Shanghai cinema, and co-director of The Spring River Flows East.
caichusheng.description: A leading director at the Lianhua studio in the 1930s, he made melodramas about fishermen, workers and modern women, and after the war co-directed the two-part family epic The Spring River Flows East with Zheng Junli.

facts.text: Song of the Fishermen was the first Chinese film to win a prize abroad, at the Moscow film festival of 1935.
The Spring River Flows East cuts between a wife's poverty in occupied Shanghai and her husband's new life in wartime Chongqing.

sunyu.signature: Lianhua's 'poet director', whose silent films joined romance to social and patriotic causes.
sunyu.description: Trained in the United States, he returned to Shanghai and made lyrical films at Lianhua about workers, peasants and young women, several ending in calls to resist Japan.

facts.text: Studied theatre and film in the United States in the 1920s.
His 1950 film The Life of Wu Xun was denounced in 1951 in an editorial written by Mao Zedong.

wuyonggang.signature: Directed The Goddess, the best-known film of China's silent era.
wuyonggang.description: A set designer who turned director at Lianhua, he made The Goddess, about a woman who sells herself to pay for her son's schooling, with Ruan Lingyu in the lead.

facts.text: Worked as a set designer in Shanghai studios before he directed.
Stanley Kwan's Center Stage (1991) restages scenes from The Goddess.

yuanmuzhi.signature: His Street Angel mixes songs, slapstick and tragedy in the alleys of 1930s Shanghai.
yuanmuzhi.description: An actor and critic who directed two films: Scenes of City Life, a satirical musical, and Street Angel, with Zhou Xuan and Zhao Dan as poor lovers in a Shanghai tenement. After 1949 he led the new state's film bureau.

facts.text: Zhou Xuan's songs from Street Angel became hits across the Chinese-speaking world.
Became the first head of the Film Bureau of the People's Republic of China in 1949.
